Donnarumma was nowhere to be seen on the corner, flapping at fresh air. No Forest player was there to apply the finish at the back post. That hint of defensive instability at City remains.

Chants of “you’re going down with United” and “you’re going down with the Derby’ from the Forest fans.

Good defending from Williams up against Ndiaye but Doku helps City keep the squeeze on.

Things break down with a careless Cherki pass in the middle of the pitch, and Forest break down their right through Delap and Munoz.

Forest’s striker did not look at all sure of himself, and is grateful for a corner.

Milenkovic with more good defending, this time intercepting a Cherki flick around the corner, before Forest do well to keep possession. A stretching run in behind by Delap prompts Dias to cover across and concede a throw in City’s half.

The Forest found themselves an open City defence again after Gibbs-White picked up the scraps off Delap, but McAtee did neither one thing nor the other, and Donnarumma claimed.

Crucial block by Milenkovic to deny Doku after a sweeping City move, the left-winger was teed up by a clever pull-back by Ndiaye from the right. Great start to the game, it is set up perfectly now.

What a start for Forest, they have finally scored a home goal this season as the clock ticks past five minutes. It was really slack from Gvardiol, dallying on the ball and drifting aimlessly infield. Cunha picked his pocket and the defender carried the ball towards the box. He had passing options left and right, but kept his head while unopposed and rolled the ball beyond Donnarumma with his left foot.

Forest have scored their first goal at the City Ground since the final game of last season. That is a drought of almost eight and a half hours.

Jair Cunha BRILLIANTLY slots home his first goal for Nottingham Forest to give them the lead against Manchester City! 💥 https://t.co/HcP4txscTK

Bright start from the home team. James McAtee with some neat close control, before Delap drifts in behind Gvardiol. A long Forest through flicks off the head of Cunha and into the gloves of Donnarumma.

City then establish some possession, with Gvardiol advanced and playing inside Doku in a narrow position.

Evangelos Marinakis, the Forest owner, is at the City Ground today in his first appearance of the season.

Marinakis has been busy with his various other business interests but is here this evening.

As a very superstitious man, can his return bring Forest some good fortune?

Just like the lyrics of Forest’s Mull of Kintyre-inspired pre-match song, there really is a mist rolling in from the Trent on a crisp autumnal evening.

Remembrance Day will be marked just before kick-off.

Even a City win today will have them three points behind Arsenal for the international break.

The margins for error are very small in title races and who knows how damaging those two successive league defeats could be for Enzo Maresca.

There is, of course, their feud with the Premier League over the guilty verdict for breaking financial rules which could render everything irrelevant.

It really is a poor situation for both City and the governing body. The whole season feels phoney and paralysed with uncertainty.

Very warm reception for Elliot Anderson from the Forest fans as he runs to the tunnel leading to the dressing rooms.

Anderson was at Forest for two seasons before that £116m move to Manchester City.

Man City will be hoping to close the gap on Arsenal to three points at the top of the table after the north London side’s 1-0 win over Hull City this afternoon.

While matters off the pitch may suggest otherwise, on it, City look the most likely side to deny Mikel Arteta’s men a second successive league title.

The two teams currently share the same goal difference (10), but City have conceded twice as many goals as Arsenal, something Maresca will be hoping to address.

From the current top eight in the league, only Chelsea have conceded more.

Forest are yet to score at home in any competition this season and have netted only six league goals in total from an xG of 14.34.

That underperformance of 8.34 goals is the biggest of any team in the Premier League this season, and of any side after nine Premier League games since at least 2021-22.

Forest come into this evening’s game in 19th, but they are just a point behind Crystal Palace and Manchester United, while victory would also take them above Coventry City and up to 16th.

Forest’s results at the City Ground have to improve quickly or this team will be in serious trouble.

They have gone almost eight and a half hours without scoring in front of their own supporters.

Forest have only recorded two home wins in the Premier League over the past 11 months which, quite frankly, is relegation form.

Oliver Glasner has played down the significance of his warning to Nottingham Forest’s squad after their defeat at Brentford has had the desired impact.

The Austrian said last weekend there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

Speaking this week, he said: “I didn’t attack anyone directly. We share that we want to be successful and win games. It was not a problem.

“It was much louder outside than I felt it was inside. This is just how I see a relationship has to be. Let’s talk about things if we don’t like things.

“If you never say anything in your relationship with your wife or children, then they will never know. Then I can’t blame somebody because if they don’t know, how can you expect things to change?

“We are now in a society where criticism or the way I talk is negative, but the intention was positive and to change to get better results so that we can all have a better life.”

Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has made three errors leading to goals this season, “recognises that he has made some mistakes,” Enzo Maresca said this week, “but at the same time recognises that he has made some great saves”.

The City manager added: “It is quite easy with him because he recognises any mistake immediately. I’ve spoken to him about it, but I didn’t feel the need to be so deep with him because he already knows and recognises that he has made some mistakes.”

Asked about City players adapting to his philosophy, Maresca said: “I can see my playing style just by working every day with them, but we can still improve many things.

“We know exactly what we are doing well and what we need to improve. It is just a matter of time.”

Elsewhere this afternoon, Martin Odegaard has broken the deadlock at the Emirates to give Arsenal a 1-0 lead over Hull City.

Victory would take Mikel Arteta’s side six points clear of City at the top of the table before this evening’s contest at the City Ground.

With around 10 minutes remaining in north London, you can follow our updates of that match here.

Erling Haaland will be hoping for his 10th league goal in 10 games this term, having bagged nine from nine so far.

Last week’s 1-0 defeat against Brighton was the first league game he failed to score in since the opening match of the season against Bournemouth.

The Norwegian is once again leading the way in the Premier League’s scoring charts, with three goals more than his nearest rivals.

Oliver Glasner pressed the nuclear button last weekend and the big question today is how his Forest players respond.

After the 2-0 defeat at Brentford, Glasner warned there would be “no compromises” and insisted his players have to fully buy into his philosophy.

This usually goes one of two ways and Glasner will be hoping it produces a positive reaction.

Training has apparently been excellent this week but it will mean little unless they transfer it into a match situation.

James McAtee has been Forest’s best player so far this season and faces the club he joined as an 11 year old.

Enzo Maresca made a flawless start at Manchester City but is now enduring a stumble.

Two successive Premier League defeats have seen City replaced at the summit by Arsenal, so the importance of this match has gone up a notch.

Elliot Anderson returns for the first time since his £116m move from Forest in the summer and what a signing he already appears.

Forest are already wondering whether their asking price should have been higher and, as daft as it sounds, City have probably got a bargain.

There will be a lot of focus today on goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma, who has been unconvincing in recent weeks.

Maresca has made three changes following City’s 3-2 win at Leipzig in midweek, with Dias, Gvardiol and Doku replacing Nunes, O’Reilly and Foden.

Glasner has made two changes to his Forest team following defeat at Brentford last weekend, with Yates and Munoz replacing Ndoye and Aina.

Is this the day the xG gods reward Nottingham Forest? Oliver Glasner’s team sit 19th having won one game all season, but there is no doubt that their performances have been significantly better than results and they might need their luck to turn against Man City team full of firepower.

Despite all of the positive indicators in Forest’s underlying data, Glasner caused some alarm with his comments after last weekend’s defeat at Brentford.

The Austrian said: “We have to accept it’s not good enough. If we lose four of the last five games, it’s not good enough. And that’s why for me, it’s now time that we change things, that I change things, and that’s what I will do.

“I feel now maybe I made too many compromises in some stuff, and it’s always compromises. It’s a clear way. I will tell [the players] what we want to do, what we have to do, and if the players buy in, I think we can have a turnaround, and if not, the sixth manager [since the start of last season] will come in.”

Dangerous words perhaps when you work for Evangelos Marinakis, but John Percy reported this week that Glasner was backed by his players in a squad meeting.

City are smarting from back-to-back defeats by Aston Villa and Brighton, but they created more than enough in both games to claim some sort of result. Nevertheless, there is a persistent sense that their defensive unit remains too marshmellow-like over the course of 38 games, and Forest have the counter-attacking threat to test them.

Glasner has happy memories of playing City, beating them in the 2025 FA Cup final with Crystal Palace, but his Forest reign is in urgent need of a signature victory and performance.

#1096. Man United’s players can’t play Mauricio Pochettino’s style – but there is a solution

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Pochettino requires an incredibly fit, mobile squad that can press with intensity and tempo, which Man United do not have. But, as Miguel Delaney explains, there could be salvation

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Mauricio Pochettino does not have much time between landing in England on Thursday afternoon and travelling to Manchester United’s greatest rivals Liverpool on Sunday but, within those three whirlwind days, he will still seek to do something that he feels just keeps everyone grounded. He will pay for a dinner out with all the players and staff.

Pochettino usually does this on the eve of every season, a custom he started in his first English job, at Southampton. Then, as now, it had to happen mid-season but at least gave him an initial sense of the squad as a group while encouraging togetherness.

It will also allow Pochettino and his staff to quicker detect the group dynamics, in lieu of an actual pre-season.

That touches on something else that Pochettino sees as a fundamental. Or, rather, the fundamental.

“The most important thing is the players’ fitness,” he said in Brave New World: Inside Pochettino’s Spurs – his 2017 book in conjunction with journalist Guillem Balague – and everything he and assistant Jesus Perez do radiates that.

It perhaps forms the single greatest issue in this season at Manchester United, and is something Pochettino himself is going to have to work out how to adapt to.

That opening meal might even be seen as the buttered carrots before the sticks used to drive these players – and regular body-fat tests.

Except, even that poses another dual-sided problem.

On one side, there is the manner the fitness of this specific squad has been questioned all season. You can go through the data or just use the eye test, to see a team regularly ripped apart. Pochettino will have to work to get them up to scratch.

But there’s then getting them up to his own levels, the standards required to really play Pochettino’s style.

As the Argentine has said, he demands his teams play “with intensity and at a high tempo”, to be “prepared for battle” in a way that provokes “a controlled disorder, to create so much movement that it distresses the opposition”.

That comes from initially distressing his own squad. Some of Pochettino’s former players have commonly remarked about how they thought they were fit, and then realised they were nowhere near what their boss actually means by that word.

Duly, the manager and Perez have their own adapted fitness exercises based on the Gacon test, named after French fitness coach Georges Gacon.

“We did a lot of them in pre-season,” Harry Kane has said.

Ben Davies talked of “crazy sessions”, that his international teammates couldn’t believe, and that then-Watford boss Quique Sanchez Flores said produced “animals”.

A further problem with United, however, is that it’s not just that Pochettino doesn’t have a pre-season. He barely has time between games. This truncated first week sets a tone. United now enter the busiest period of the season, where the Champions League group stages are at their most intense and then it’s Christmas.

Elimination from the Carabao Cup may actually be seen as a gift.

Worse, if Pochettino does attempt anything like his usual fitness approach, United’s under-cooked players are likely to break down with injuries. He is consequently going to have to adapt as much as his squad.

Pressing has long been described as the core principle of Pochettino’s game but the reality is that it is now the core principle of everyone’s game in the Premier League. Teams operate with multiple varied systems. And, as one Premier League coach says, if you get your pressing wrong, or it’s not calibrated correctly, modern teams can so easily play around you.

It is described as one of those unseen elements of the modern game that explains why teams can suddenly get badly beaten.

Pochettino did arrive in mid-season at Southampton and immediately got them pressing – to the point that Sir Alex Ferguson even commented approvingly after the Argentine’s very first game: a valiant 2-1 defeat at Old Trafford. That was nevertheless in a very different Premier League, that hadn’t properly gone through the Pep Guardiola-inspired pressing revolution. What Pochettino was doing was itself revolutionary, and he enthused about how he had “hungry players who didn’t want to be relegated”.

This is at least where his time at Paris Saint-Germain may offer necessary experience beyond weathering an immense weight of expectation.

Pochettino instantly realised that Neymar, Kylian Mbappe and later Lionel Messi just weren’t going to run or press in a way anything close to what he expected, so he essentially had to abandon his usual approach.

Eight players would instead have to compromise for the three stars. And, without a full XI running, this wasn’t a true Pochettino team.

He and Perez would still point out that they had PSG’s best Champions League performance in getting to the semi-finals in a full season – Thomas Tuchel’s final was in the Covid campaign – before the club belatedly decided to change approach. They have often remarked with a touch of envy how they would have loved to work with the youth-defined approach that Luis Enrique has enjoyed.

That may be one way Pochettino gets around these various problems. He’s spoken before about how gaps were “filled by youngsters”.

Such a commitment to youth has been another core principle of his career. And, aside from being willing to take instruction and run harder with more energy, young players also give you something else.

“There’s nothing quite like winning with the team you joined at 13 or 14 and have given your heart and soul to,” he explained in his book. “You then move on to play for the first team with a feeling of identity that offers the team an added extra. It’s something that will be stamped on every side I coach.”

It was similar at Tottenham, where Pochettino described a squad that sounds someway similar to United now – “figures who at some point in their careers had been considered stars but had lost their way. And the team didn’t come first”.

That’s what Pochettino will demand. Now, he will coach a side arguably more associated with youth than any in the game, but one thing they don’t have is time to grow.

Pochettino’s United have to hit the ground running, when running is one of the issues.

#1095. Mauricio Pochettino urges Pep Guardiola to take USA job: ‘Perfect moment’

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Guardiola has taken a sabbatical after ending a lengthy stint at Manchester City

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Outgoing US men’s national team boss Mauricio Pochettino has urged Pep Guardiola to take the job, amid widespread speculation that the Spaniard is the United States Soccer Federation’s main target.

Guardiola has taken a one-year sabbatical after ending a 10-year stint at Manchester City in the summer, while Pochettino has accepted the head coach role at Manchester United, replacing the sacked Michael Carrick.

The 54-year-old is overseeing the US’ Nations League quarter-final against Haiti, with his final match in charge coming in the second leg on Tuesday. The US won the first leg 6-0 at the weekend.

On Monday Pochettino urged Guardiola to take the job if he is offered it, although formal contact between him and the United States Soccer Federation has not been made.

Pochettino told reporters: “It's the perfect moment to arrive to the [US Soccer] Federation. Everything is in the right direction.

“I think, of course, take [it]. Take it because he's going to find really good people, good players. The player can fit for his style; the National Training Centre that wasn’t [there] before.”

The Argentine spent two years in charge of the US team and led them to the round of 16 at this summer’s World Cup.

He suggested that the fact that he was scouted for the Manchester United role indicated that managing the US team had increased its prestige and profile.

He said: “Now the vision from Europe, I promise, is completely different after the World Cup. Being head coach in USA now is prestigious.

“It's Manchester United, the calibre of [Real] Madrid, Barcelona. Manchester United is coming for the coach of the USA.

“If you start to think that if you are another coach, maybe you are not working - [Antonio] Conte, or I don't know - you say, ‘Oh, it's a great opportunity because it's not only the value of being coach here. If Pochettino from Chelsea comes here, [then goes to] Manchester United.’ The vision is completely different.”

He will travel to Old Trafford after Tuesday’s game, with his first match as Manchester United boss a trip to Liverpool in the Premier League next Sunday.

#1094. Tony Mowbray steps down as Blackburn manager due to health reasons

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Mowbray was diagnosed with bowel cancer in 2024 and had to stand down from his role at Birmingham

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Tony Mowbray has stepped down from his role as Blackburn Rovers manager due to health reasons.

Mowbray was diagnosed with bowel cancer in early 2024 and had to stand down from his role at Birmingham.

He was later given the all-clear after a spell at West Brom last year, he joined Blackburn for a second spell in June.

However, the Championship club have confirmed that he will once again be stepping away from work.

“Unfortunately, due to health issues, I have to step back from my role as Head Coach of Blackburn Rovers,” Mowbray said in a statement.

“I’m immensely proud of this group of players. Their dedication and professionalism have given us some memorable performances and wins, and I’ve loved working with them.

“Thank you to my coaching staff for all your hard work and for the support you’ve given me. It’s been a pleasure working alongside you.

“To the fans, thank you for the way you’ve supported me and the team this season. I’ve always tried to give you a team that you can be proud of. Your support has meant a great deal to me.

“I’m grateful to the Owners and Suhail [Shaikh, Blackburn COO] for giving me the opportunity to lead this great club once again.

Mowbray previously managed Blackburn for five years between 2017 and 2022, and has previously held roles at the likes of Sunderland, Coventry, Middlesbrough and Celtic.

He has sparked something of a resurgence at Ewood Park, with Blackburn finding themselves just three points off the play-offs in 13th despite going into the season touted for relegation.

"Tony's passion for the club and his professionalism are clear to see, but it is his kindness and the care he shows for players, staff and those around him that mean so much," Blackburn chief executive officer Steve Curwood added.

"Our priority now is to make sure he feels that same care and support from all of us. We will support him and his family in every way we can."

No matter what happens when they face Portugal tonight, Wales know they will face a relegation play-off, but they will want to end their Group A campaign on a high (kick-off 7:45 pm, live on BBC Two and iPlayer).

Despite picking up just three points so far, from their 2-1 home win over Norway, Wales will not be automatically relegated from the top tier, with that fate going to the two bottom sides overall and both Turkey and the Czech Republic finished without a single point.

Instead, Craig Bellamy’s side will take part in a relegation play-off in March against one of the teams from League B, with their opponents to be confirmed when the draw takes place on Friday, 20 November.

Wales would love to go out on a high, despite the disappointment of missing out on a chance to be among the top seeds for Euro 2028 qualifying.

Portugal also know their Nations League fate, but the top spot is not yet secured; they know just a point will be enough to give them the advantage going into the quarter-final draw.

They are the reigning champions after beating Spain on penalties in the 2025 final, and they have won the tournament twice after beating the Netherlands in the inaugural final back in 2019.

Despite their history, they are only the fourth favourites to lift the trophy again, with the football betting sites behind Spain, France and England.

But they are the standout favourites for this one at 5/11, while Wales are 6/1 to secure only their second win over Portugal.

They have only met five times, and Wales’ only win came back in 1951, when they secured a 2-1 win in Cardiff. Since then, they have lost three games in a row without scoring a single goal, including back in September when Joao Felix scored the only goal of the game in Lisbon.

Wales managed just one shot on target in that one, and goals have been a problem for Bellamy’s side, with just three in their five Nations League goals and eight conceded.

Jorge Jesus’ side, on the other hand, have scored 10 but they do go into the game on the back of a surprise 4-1 drubbing at home by Denmark, and they will want to prove that they can cope without their talisman Cristiano Ronaldo, who retired from international duty earlier this month.

Wales have now lost five of their last six games in all competitions, which is as many defeats as they had in their previous 29 matches, and it’s hard to see them getting anything out of this one.

Former Chelsea midfielder Joao Felix has scored three goals in Portugal’s Nations League campaign, including the winner when the two sides last met.

The 27-year-old left Stamford Bridge in the summer of 2025, moving to Saudi side Al-Nassr for a fee of £43.7m, where he joined up with then Portuguese captain Ronaldo.

With a Ronaldo-sized void to fill Felix has shown what he is capable of and betting sites are offering 11/8 on him scoring at any time or 5/1 on him scoring first or last, and he has done twice each during this campaign.

#1090. Inside Calciopoli, the match-fixing bombshell that brought Juventus to its knees

Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation plus sign you up to our newsletter.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

The 2006 match-fixing controversy exposed corruption at the very top of Serie A – at its centre was one man and his mobile phone

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

At the time, it was called “the biggest scandal in the history of European football” – a sporting earthquake that was off the Richter scale. Dubbed by some onlookers as ‘Moggi-gate', it became more widely known as Calciopoli, a match-fixing scandal that dominated Italian football and overshadowed the Azzurri's 2006 World Cup success.

It resulted in Italy's richest and most decorated football club, Juventus, being kicked out of Serie A, despite many saying that, given the club's connection to the powerful Agnelli family – the owners of Fiat motors – such a thing could never happen. Of the other clubs charged with match-fixing, Milan, Lazio and Fiorentina were each deducted 30 points for the 2005-06 season, even if they were allowed to hang on to their Serie A status. The Rossoneri still finished third and qualified for the Champions League, despite their tally falling to 58.

What exactly was Calciopoli and how was it allowed to come about? Who were the power-brokers that made up Luciano Moggi's network? In the months that followed, the scandal left far more questions than answers.

In understanding it all, the logical place to start is with Moggi, the man whose name became synonymous with football corruption. A former railway stationmaster from Tuscany, he was one of the most controversial figures in Italian football for more than 20 years. He started out as a talent scout for Juventus, then had periods as sporting director at Roma, Lazio, Torino and Napoli, before returning to Juve in 1994.

During that period, Moggi began to weave his web of useful contacts. His methods were controversial and he was tagged ‘Lucky Luciano' after surviving a number of investigations, including claims that he laid on prostitutes for referees in UEFA Cup games while at Torino – claims that he denied.

Back at Juventus, the trophies began to pile up, but players and fans of rival clubs suspected that Moggi was using his weighty book of contacts to influence results. Everyone in the game had a story about Moggi, but no-one could prove anything. Moggi himself revelled in the mystique his power had created, sometimes jokingly referring to himself as ‘The Devil'.

The suspicions, it was later discovered, were not completely unfounded. The findings of an Italian Football Federation tribunal claimed that, making more than 400 phone calls a day, Moggi controlled referees, as well as having federation bosses and television presenters in his pocket.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

His downfall came through intercepted calls. The Turin magistrates, who had brought criminal charges against Juve's managing director Antonio Giraudo and club doctor Riccardo Agricola for alleged doping offences (Giraudo was acquitted at the initial trial, while Agricola's charges were later thrown out by the Appeal Court), tapped the phones of the club's directors for 48 days in 2004.

What the magistrates heard was of no use to their inquiry, but they passed the transcripts on to the football federation and to magistrates in Naples, who separately had been investigating links between football and organised crime in the south of Italy. The Naples magistrates tapped the phones of dozens of people from the world of football for the 2004-05 season and Moggi-gate exploded in early May 2006, when excerpts from those two sets of phone taps were leaked to the press.

The selection of referees for games in Serie A was entrusted to two ‘designators': Paolo Bergamo and Pierluigi Pairetto. The names of referees were sorted into groups, according to experience. Then, in theory, they were drawn, lottery-style, and matched up with the weekend's fixtures.

The evidence from the first wave of leaks suggested that not only was the selection of referees for Serie A matches not as random as it should have been but, even more alarmingly, that Moggi held some sway over the choice of refs for Juve's Champions League games via Pairetto, who was also a member of the UEFA referees' committee. Before Juventus travelled to face Ajax in Amsterdam on September 15, 2004, Pairetto phoned Moggi.

PAIRETTO: I know that you've forgotten about me but I haven't forgotten about you.

PAIRETTO: I've put a great referee for the game in Amsterdam.

PAIRETTO: Anyway, it was just to tell you this. You see, I remember about you.

The referee was the Swiss, Urs Meier, most famous in England for being in charge of the Three Lions' quarter-final loss to Portugal at Euro 2004. Juventus beat Ajax 1-0. There has never been any suggestion that Meier was in on the arrangement or acted at all improperly. It was by no means the first time that Moggi and Pairetto had spoken. After Juventus had drawn 2-2 at home to Swedish club Djurgarden in a Champions League qualifier the previous month, in which German referee Herbert Fandel disallowed a goal by Juve's Fabrizio Miccoli, Moggi had angrily disapproved.

MOGGI: What the f**k kind of referee did you send us?

MOGGI: It was valid, it was valid. He can f**k himself. I have to make the return match in Stockholm secure, no? With another like [Fandel], it's going to be a bit difficult, no? You follow me?

Juve won the return leg in Stockholm 4-1, with Graham Poll refereeing. Again, there has never been any suggestion that Poll was aware of the relationship between Moggi and Pairetto or acted improperly. After the match, Moggi clearly had nothing to grumble about, but the appointment of Poll had come as a surprise to him. Two days before the game, Lucky Luciano called the secretary of the Italian football league.

SECRETARY: I've got Graham Poll written here.

PAIRETTO: Well something has happened at the last minute, he was sick or something.

PAIRETTO: Yes, yes. I'll look into it right away.

For domestic games, investigators claimed that by rigging what was supposed to be a random draw, Pairetto and Bergamo could choose from a pool of referees who were considered to be pro-Juventus. Massimo de Santis had been due to officiate at the 2006 World Cup until the scandal broke, after which he was hurriedly withdrawn by the Italian Football Federation.

It was later claimed that the referees in the ‘pro-Juve pool' would give Moggi's men the benefit of the doubt in most situations, award non-existent penalties or deny the opposition blatant ones, and disallow perfectly good goals. They would use different criteria for Juventus and their opponents when deciding what merited a yellow card – most seasons, the Turin club had the lowest yellow cards to fouls ratio.

Sometimes they would be assigned to a game featuring a team that was due to play against Juve the following week. In those games, it was claimed that their job was to book or send off key players so they would be suspended by the time they faced Juventus.

They were not being paid for their favours or receiving lavish gifts. The system was much simpler. Investigators alleged that it was made clear to refs by Pairetto and Bergamo that if they wanted to get on, wanted to take charge of the big games, to have a career, they had to toe the line. Moggi also had a contact on the inside, Italian football federation vice president Innocenzo Mazzini, according to the investigation.

When the Italian federation opened disciplinary hearings, Moggi's network was described as a “sophisticated system which undermined one of the fundamental principles of sport: the independence of referees”.

Investigators alleged that Moggi also controlled what some television programmes said about the referees, to temper any public backlash against controversial decisions that had gone in favour of Juventus. The approach was subtle – the presenters were only to take Juve's side in situations where there had been a close call. If a foul or penalty was obvious to everyone, it would have been counter-productive to pretend it hadn't happened.

The following wiretap conversation, as later translated by a University of Perugia report, was between Moggi and Fabio Baldas, a former referee who was an expert pundit on a television programme called Il processo di Biscardi.

According to investigators, the pair spoke before nearly every programme to discuss what was going to be said, but Baldas received criticism from fans for taking Juventus' side when he analysed a controversial decision made by an official during a match.

BALDAS: I tried to defend myself, but they attacked me from all sides and said I was a Juventus fan!

[Since this article was first published in FourFourTwo magazine in 2006, criminal proceedings against almost all the journalists caught up in the wiretaps were dropped in 2007, although several were suspended by Italy's Order of Journalists]

Lazio and Fiorentina were both run by businessmen who were new to football: Claudio Lotito and Diego Della Valle. The two men sensed there was something rotten in the state of the Italian game from the moment they arrived on the scene. Lotito talked about “moralising” the sport, while Della Valle attacked the system of selling TV rights, which ensured the big three – Juve, Milan and Inter – earned fortunes and everyone else shared the rest.

Key decisions seemed to go against their teams – as the 2004-05 season drew to a close, they were heading towards the trapdoor to Serie B. What to do? Go down with your principles still intact? Get real.

According to prosecutor Stefano Palazzi, phone taps showed that Lotito asked federation president Franco Carraro for help in four end-of-season matches. Carraro told ref designator Bergamo that he should “give Lazio a hand”. Fiorentina asked Mazzini for help in two vital relegation games.

Unfortunately for the two clubs, the federation's sporting code makes no allowance for acting in self-defence. Attempting to alter the outcome of a game is an offence and the two clubs were later hit with 30-point deductions for 2005-06, with more points docked for the following campaign.

They argued that in comparison to Juventus they'd done nothing, but the trio of clubs relegated in 2004-05 – Bologna, Brescia and Atalanta – were unsympathetic. They also knew how the system worked, but asked no favours and went down playing football.

Quite why Milan ever got involved is a mystery. Perhaps they realised what Juventus were up to and felt they were being denied titles that were rightfully theirs. Palazzi accused Adriano Galliani, Milan's vice-president, of backing the dodgy operations of the club's referees' assistant, Leonardo Meani: “Meani was in phone contact with linesmen, who were asked, when in doubt, to favour Milan, and Galliani approved.”

As Milan's links with friendly linesmen became public, the joke within Italian football circles was that Juve controlled the refs and Milan the linesmen, while Inter – perennial underachievers at that stage – controlled the ball boys.

By the end of May 2006, Carraro and Mazzini had resigned from the Italian federation and were joined by Pairetto and Bergamo. On July 14, five days after Italy's victory in the World Cup final, the federation's disciplinary tribunal handed out sentences:

Later, appeals further softened many of the penalties. Juventus remained in Serie B but with only nine points docked. They were stripped of two titles – the 2004-05 Scudetto was not reassigned to another club, but the 2005-06 title was awarded to Inter, making them champions for the first time since 1989.

Lazio and Fiorentina were back in Serie A, docked three and 15 points respectively for the 2006-07 season, plus 30 each for 2005-06. Milan had the same punishment for 2005-06, as well as eight deducted for 2006-07. Carraro's ban was reduced to an €80,000 fine.

The reduced sentences caused outrage. Giovanni Semeraro, president of Lecce, one of the clubs relegated in 2005-06, said: “It's something to be ashamed of, no?”

The verdicts had come against a background of increasing calls for clemency, or even a total amnesty, on the grounds that it wouldn't be fair to punish the clubs that had provided so many of Italy's World Cup winners. Populist politicians from both sides of parliament lined up to argue for mercy, and they were backed by the mayors of Rome, Turin and Florence. A member of the appeals panel admitted that the panel had also been worried about a violent reaction from fans if three teams – Juventus, Fiorentina and Lazio – had been kicked out of Serie A.

There were other factors in the softening of sentences. Lazio's case was strengthened considerably when the club was allowed to call as a witness Daniele Tombolini, the referee who had been in charge of Lazio vs Brescia, one of the games in which the Rome club was alleged to have sought favours. Tombolini told the appeals tribunal that, far from giving Lazio a hand, he'd made mistakes in the game that had favoured Brescia.

Milan appeared to have convinced the appeals tribunal that its referees' assistant, Leonardo Meani, had collaborated independently, and for whose actions the club should not be held directly responsible.

There remained an enigma at the heart of the matter. Moggi was widely recognised as a master of the transfer market. He'd never played at a high level, but had an eye for a player and discovered many who would go on to become legends. At Juve, he finally had the financial clout to hire Italy's best coaches and the world's top players.

By ‘signing up' referees, journalists and federation officials to the club's cause as well, according to investigators, he was admitting that the best wasn't good enough – a surprising lack of faith in his own abilities and an insult to a generation of great footballers, from Alessandro Del Piero to Zinedine Zidane.

Moggi continued to protest innocence, though, seeing himself as a scapegoat who had been ritually sacrificed to pay for the sins of an entire system, with no intention of going quietly.

Bayern Munich CEO Karl-Heinz Rummenigge probably spoke for many in European football when he said in August 2006: “I feel sorry for Juventus, but the important thing is that people like Moggi are not around any more.” Asked whether he would return to football, Moggi told the newspaper Repubblica: “Of course, but this time I'm going to be the guy who breaks everybody's balls. I'll finger them all, by their first names and surnames. I'll break the balls of all the false moralists who think that everything is clean now because they got rid of Luciano Moggi.”

This feature first appeared in the October 2006 issue of FourFourTwo

In June 2011, shortly before the expiry of his five-year suspension from football, Luciano Moggi was banned for life by the Italian Football Federation. Six months after that, Moggi was sentenced to five years and four months in prison for his part in the match-fixing scandal, although that was later reduced to two years and four months on appeal.

The jail term was then cancelled in 2015, when a court ruled that the statute of limitations had expired, though he wasn’t acquitted either.

After being demoted in 2006, Juventus overcame their nine-point deduction to win Serie B at the first attempt, aided by 20 goals from Alessandro Del Piero, who remained with the club. They finished third in their first campaign back in the top flight, before becoming champions once more in 2012, beginning a run of nine successive Serie A title wins.

The stain of Calciopoli never entirely left though – once the world’s finest league, Serie A now trails significantly behind its European rivals.

#1089. Wayne Rooney says he contemplated suicide during ‘lowest point’ of Man Utd career

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Rooney said he would spend two days at a time drinking at home during his lowest points

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Wayne Rooney has revealed there was a period in his Manchester United career where he contemplated suicide.

The former England striker said that, even as he flourished on the pitch, his mental health was suffering off it, despite being newly married and a dad to his eldest child, Kai.

He would spend two days at a time drinking at home and, he told the ‘Life At The Midpoint with Gabby Logan’ podcast, at his lowest point considered taking his own life.

“I can look back and say I was selfish, but I knew I was going through something which I was really struggling to deal with. Then I didn’t want Kai seeing me like that, so that’s why I’d hide away as well,” Rooney said.

“I got to a place where you’re contemplating suicide. You just didn’t want to be around anyone. I didn’t want to be see people in the streets. I didn’t want to go into shops.

“I was always comfortable on a football pitch, but everything else [I] really struggled with it.”

Rooney, United’s all-time record goalscorer, said the issues he faced occurred at the height of his Red Devils career.

“You don’t want to show any weakness, so you try to mask it,” he added.

“Even though I knew the position I was in, it was difficult to actually admit that I was in that in that position because I felt like you feel less of a man if you like for doing that.

“I was speaking to a therapist to try and figure out what was up with me because when I look back I was probably at the height of my career, I’ve just had a young son, I’ve just been married. It should be the happiest point in my life and it wasn’t.

“It was probably the lowest point because of the selfish acts I was taking.”

Rooney, who is currently featuring in ITV reality programme ‘I’m A Celebrity… Get Me Out Of Here’, credits his wife Coleen with helping him turn the tide.

“Coleen helped me massively. She could have walked away, it was that bad, but she stuck by me and helped me get through it,” he said.

#1088. Secrets of the vampires: genomes reveal how these bats live off blood alone

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

All the better to eat you with: vampire bats (such as this common vampire bat, Desmodus rotundus) have an array of genetic adaptations that allow them to subsist on blood.Credit: Joel Sartore/Photo Ark/Nature Picture Library

A foraging vampire bat slices into sleeping prey and laps up about half of its own body weight in blood, causing its belly to balloon. Now, an analysis of the bats’ genomes and organs offers clues to how they stomach this gory diet.

The study1, posted on the preprint server bioRxiv on 7 November before being peer reviewed, provides a “high-resolution look into what it takes to build a vampire bat”, says Jasmin Camacho, an evolutionary developmental biologist at the Stowers Institute for Medical Research in Kansas City, Missouri, who was not involved in the research. “It’s one of the first times we can really see what those molecular signatures of being a blood specialist look like.”

Blood is a challenging meal: it contains mostly water, little sugar and fat, and toxic amounts of iron. Yet all three species of vampire bat survive exclusively on blood after reaching adulthood.

To understand how they pull this off, Michael Hiller, an evolutionary genomicist at the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, and his colleagues generated genomes for all three vampire-bat species (Desmodus rotundus, Diaemus youngii and Diphylla ecaudata) and three other species of bat. They then compared the genomes. They also analysed gene activity in six organs for two of the vampire species and four species of non-vampiric bats.

The stomach stood out. In most mammals, the stomach bathes food in acid to aid digestion. In vampire bats, however, the researchers found that the organ has been repurposed into a stretchy, pH-neutral storage sac lined with thick layers of connective tissue that help it to expand after a feast.

Vampire bats’ stomachs can expand enormously to accommodate their meals of blood. Credit: Jon Flanders

To shed excess water quickly so that the bats can fly home, their stomachs ramp up activity of a fluid-transporting gene that is typically active in salivary and sweat glands by more than 900-fold, the analysis found. The function of these vampire-bat stomachs has changed so much from those of other mammals that the organs perhaps “deserve a different name”, Hiller says.

Despite the lack of fat in blood, the bats still retain some genes for digesting lipids. The activity of these genes is dialled down in adulthood but might enable nursing pups to digest their mother’s fat-rich milk before switching to blood after weaning, says Ken Welch Jr, a comparative physiologist at the University of Toronto in Canada. But the bats have lost some genes altogether, such as ones known to help animals to distinguish between sweet and bitter tastes2.

#1087. Liverpool’s expensive attack feast on Palace to leave Sage looking doomed

Crystal Palace are playing this season as if afflicted by a curse. They seem to have made a terrible deal, possibly involving a monkey’s paw. As a result, Pierre Sage’s team were able to defend credibly for around 44 minutes of each half, on one condition: They must switch off completely, at least twice per game.

This being the Premier League, those lapses in concentration are usually punished. A mostly compact performance out of possession briefly became as porous as a bath sponge when Liverpool eased into a 2-0 lead, nine minutes after half-time. Florian Wirtz did not even need to finish cleanly to score his first Premier League goal of the season, striding on to an unopposed low cross from Bradley Barcola and killing the match as a contest.

Bradley Barcola and Florian Wirtz combine to put Liverpool 2-0 up! 🔴 https://t.co/F6sw33FkYZ

Major signings need to lay down a marker when arriving at Liverpool. Barcola has his hat-trick at LASK in the Champions League, but we are still waiting for a stirring big-match-defining contribution from him since his summer arrival. Arguably the same could be said for Wirtz, nearly 18 months since he joined.

Neither left Selhurst Park looking like the world-beaters they did occasionally for their previous clubs. Still, one misfiring attacker creating a goal for another represents progress and all great partnerships must start somewhere. Lennon and McCartney would improve after 1958’s Too Bad About Sorrows.

If there was ever a place for the least-productive expensively assembled attacking group in the league to find form it was surely south London on this Sunday lunchtime. Liverpool came in with two defeats in their previous two but, European trophy aside, it has been a lousy 2026 for Palace.

They have the most defeats of any ever-present Premier League team and began (and ended) the weekend with the worst defensive record. They have conceded twice as many goals from headers as any other team. Even their most loyal fan group has disbanded.

Alexis Mac Allister opened the scoring in gut-punching fashion, after a series of Palace near-misses. Chairman Steve Parish rubbed his face in the directors’ box, in the style of peak-stress era Guardiola. None of this looked good for Sage, who appears on the brink of dismissal, with Thomas Frank his most likely replacement.

Asked if he expected to remain in his job on the other side of the international break Sage said he deemed his prospects “better than you, I think”.

“We deserved better today,” the Frenchman said. “But football is not about what you deserve it is about how efficient you are and today we had a lack of efficiency”.

Counter-intuitively, it was Palace’s flashes of promise which suggested the Frenchman might be doomed. There is enough to work with here, and plenty going marginally against Palace to suggest a change in leadership might prompt a turnaround, however unfair it would be on their manager. Yéremy Pino hit the bar, Jorgen Strand Larsen had his composed close-range goal struck from the record by VAR, Daichi Kamada stung Alisson Becker’s palms and the Brazilian saved well again from Adam Wharton’s feathered header.

Jorgen Strand Larsen thought he had the opener against Liverpool, but it was ruled out for offside! ❌ https://t.co/JkSKbtkvak

The other factor which seems likely to condemn Sage is his team’s boneheaded defensive lapses. Liverpool were awarded a debatable free-kick out wide, Quinten Timber let Mac Allister run off him too easily and he duly nodded Dominik Szoboszlai’s delivery past Dean Henderson with ease. Another header conceded.

Liverpool have taken the lead against Crystal Palace thanks to Alexis Mac Alister's header! 💥 https://t.co/kNal7qsQ35

Mac Allister, formerly of Brighton, endeared himself to the Holmesdale Road Stand with a priggish celebration. There was some blowback from the seats closest, but a more dominant sense of resignation. Someone in the adjoining block took out their phone and snapped a picture. Formerly hated rival scoring against you, rubbing it in with his celebration: truly one to show the grandkids.

Liverpool had put together little of substance until then, with Wirtz drifting through another half, Alexander Isak looking keen but flawed and Barcola spooning a promising shot into low-Earth orbit. The second half was better, but Isak looked to have wasted his best chance, a one-on-one with Henderson thumped too close to the goalkeeper.

Isak had his moment in the end, checking back to finish calmly at the end of a counter-attack against a tiring defence. Eight for the season for him and an assist for Wirtz, too, although it was hardly a pass of Molbyesque majesty.

“Happy for him,” Iraola said of Wirtz, also praising Isak’s movement for the German’s goal. “I think [Wirtz] has been very unlucky in the Premier League, a couple of goals disallowed and situations where he deserves honestly to score.”

So it was Liverpool’s blip righted here, despite all of Palace’s pressure. Alisson, who took some flak for his performance at Fenerbahce, was hard to fault. He may not have reached Eddie Nketiah’s stoppage-time penalty, but made a series of brave saves and deserved a clean sheet. For all that attacking talent, the long-serving goalkeeper still looks like one of Iraola’s most important players.

Good afternoon and welcome to our live coverage of this Premier League match between Crystal Palace and Liverpool at Selhurst Park.

The pressure is building on Palace head coach Pierre Sage, who desperately needs a win to lift the mood and propel the club out of the relegation zone. Nottingham Forest’s impressive 3-1 win over Manchester City on Saturday evening means that Palace have dropped to a lowly 19th and are two points from safety. To make matters worse, Sage’s beleaguered side have also conceded the most goals in the division (21 in nine games).

On Thursday night, Daichi Kamada’s stoppage-time equaliser rescued a 1-1 home draw in the Europa League against Hoffenheim, after Palace delivered an alarmingly lacklustre performance.

Meanwhile, Liverpool also endured midweek European torment, as Andoni Iraola’s men fell to an error-ridden 3-2 defeat away at Fenerbahce in the Champions League, having previously lost 1-0 to Arsenal in their most recent Premier League encounter on Merseyside last weekend, which has left the club in sixth but just five points behind second-place Man City.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Iraola said: “I think that’s the challenge, especially in a club like Liverpool. One week ago in this same press conference, we were on a run, everything was in a good place and we were in a better mood. And now, two defeats, it changes. It has to change and it has to be like this in a club like ours. Now we have to react after two defeats.”

As for Palace’s team news, Jean-Philippe Mateta is serving the first match of a three-game domestic ban after he was sent off for Palace in the 2-0 defeat to Tottenham last time out in the league. Liverpool’s long-term absentees include Hugo Ekitike, Giovanni Leoni, Conor Bradley and Jeremie Frimpong, while Ryan Gravenberch could also miss out after struggling with a heel injury.

Kick-off is at 14:00, with team news arriving shortly.

#1085. Juventus midfielder admits Mauricio Pochettino could sign United States players at Man United

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Weston McKennie has suggested several USMNT players could follow the Argentine to Old Trafford

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Juventus midfielder Weston McKennie has suggested several US players could follow outgoing boss Mauricio Pochettino to Manchester United, after the Argentine succeeded the sacked Michael Carrick as head coach.

Pochettino has remained with the USMNT squad for their Nations League fixtures in this international window, both against Haiti, before he heads for Old Trafford.

And McKennie suggested several players could potentially follow the manager as he sets about a rebuild of the struggling side, who are currently in the Premier League relegation zone.

Speaking at a press conference, McKennie said: “USMNT players at Manchester United? I think that, obviously, the time Pochettino spent here allowed him to appreciate this squad and see the quality it has to offer.

“And yes, I think it's a possibility. We have a lot of guys on this team who will probably make a move soon or within the next year. So I think the links are somewhat inevitable.

“At the end of the day, though, you never know what's going through a manager’s head or what kind of players he's looking for.

“Still, I think you could see a few of us linked with United, and maybe it will actually happen.”

Pochettino is taking several of his staff with him to United, with goalkeeper coach Toni Jimenez, assistant Jesus Perez and fitness coach Sebastian Pochettino having already left for England after the US’ 6-0 victory over Haiti on Saturday.

Assistant coach Miguel D’Agostino, fitness coach Sylvia Tuya Vinas and analyst Alex Scott will follow them after Tuesday’s second leg of the quarter-finals.

Pochettino said on Monday: “That was the plan when we agreed terms with Manchester United and with the national team. They are preparing all there because Wednesday when we arrive, it’s going to be nonstop, and then start with playing games. We are focused here into finishing the best way.”

For his part, the former Southampton, Tottenham and Chelsea boss refused to be drawn into speculation over whether he will sign some of his former US charges in the winter transfer window.

He said: “All the good players always have dreams to reach the (highest) level, and United is one of the teams in that level.

“In case some decisions need to be made, we are going to pay attention to the players we know really well.”

In the mid-2000s, Freddy Adu was earmarked as the next big thing in world football.

After making his professional debut as a 14-year-old for D.C. United in 2004, he became the youngest ever player to appear in professional sports in the United States. His international debut came at the age of 16, amid reported interest from some of Europe’s biggest clubs.

But the career that followed was a nomadic one, as his progress stalled and Adu would turn into something of a globetrotter in search of fresh opportunities.

This saw the American take in stints in Portugal, France, Greece and Serbia amongst other places, but Adu believes that a key issue with his career was the fact that these teams were often more interested in the marketing buzz that signing him would generate, rather than handing him opportunities on the pitch.

“I’d sign for teams, then you’d find out they were just trying to use you for the marketing part of it, to get eyeballs on their team,” Adu tells FourFourTwo.

“Then when you’re not playing for that team, it’s like ‘Why am I here? I’m living in a different country, I’m trying to get my career going and I’m not getting a chance to play’.

“At some point, you just figure out ‘This isn’t going to work out’.”

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

For Adu, the mixed messages from clubs he signed for would prove to be extremely frustrating at times when he was looking to get his career back on track.

|There were so many different places where the front office wanted you, but the coach had different ideas,” he adds. “I’d been brought in under false pretences.

“Then you go to another team, sometimes you’re playing and it works out at the start, but then it doesn’t work out.

“After a while, it wasn’t fun any more, you start losing confidence in yourself, like ‘How am I here, and how am I not getting a chance to play here?’ You start questioning the reasons why you were brought in.”

For Adu, this cycle began in 2008, when Monaco brought him in initially on loan from Benfica for the 2008/09 season, before declining to make the move permanent at the end of that campaign.

“The whole thing started when I was in Monaco – the president wanted to bring me in, I knew him, I was cool with him, but the coach had different ideas.”

Emi Martinez is poised for a return to action on Tuesday night in a huge boost for Chelsea.

The 34-year-old goalkeeper underwent surgery after fracturing his jaw during Chelsea’s 2-0 win at Everton in October, though manager Xabi Alonso revealed he was ahead of schedule in his recovery when he returned to training earlier this month.

Despite not playing a minute since suffering the injury, Martinez was called up Lionel Scaloni for Argentina’s November internationals.

And after not featuring in the 2-1 defeat to Uruguay on Friday, Scaloni confirmed that Martinez will be start in between the sticks for a friendly against Costa Rica in Cordoba.

“Emiliano is going ⁠to play in goal, he'll be there," Scaloni told reporters.

"Maybe he was fit for the previous match, ‌but it was a risk, ​and since we trust ‌Gero [Geronimo Rulli], Juan [Musso] ⁠and Santi [Santiago Beltran], we ⁠chose to look after him. An extra ‌three ​days was a ‌prudent choice."

Martinez was in contention to feature for Chelsea in their last match before the international break, but Alonso opted for deputy Mike Penders as the Blues lost 1-0 to Sunderland in contentious fashion.

Chelsea have won one and lost three during 21-year-old Penders’ run in goal, though the highly-rated Belgian keeper did impress in a 2-0 win over Manchester United at the end of October.

Martinez’s return to action will likely spell the end for Penders’ stint, though, with the Argentinian now on course to start for Chelsea when they host Leeds on Saturday.

The Liverpool legend succeeded Joe Fagan in the Anfield dugout

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

By 1985, Kenny Dalglish had already established himself as an all-time Liverpool great.

But after eight years as being the Reds’ talismanic force on the pitch, Dalglish was handed the opportunity to play an even bigger role at the club, when he was asked to succeed manager Joe Fagan.

While Dalglish would excel in his new dual player-manager position, it was not a role he had expected to take on, but he admits he was unable to refuse the offer.

“I don't know why the club asked me to become player-manager in 1985,” the Scot tells FourFourTwo.

“But they did, so I said, ‘OK, no problem for me. If that's what you want, I'll have a go.’”

For Dalglish, it was the structure and culture of the club that made what would be a daunting transition more manageable.

“The people around me were important – there was a vast experience in that dressing room, with the coaching staff, and Bob Paisley came back to help,” he continues.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“He was fantastic. The people upstairs, the chief executive, they'd do all the negotiations for wages and transfers, I didn't want to be involved in money. It was really well organised.”

This backing from everyone in the club allowed Dalglish to focus on the on-pitch matters.

“They said, ‘All you can do is be your best' – to come out of the dressing room and sit in the manager's office, those were my team-mates and it was tough at times, but it wasn't something that you could turn down,” he adds.

And Dalglish’s best would prove to be more than good enough, as he would win the first of three league titles as manager of Liverpool in that very first season in his new role.

#1081. Fan who racially abused Kylian Mbappe at LaLiga match avoids prison time

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

The fan abused Mbappe during Real Madrid’s win at Real Oviedo in August 2025

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

A fan who racially abused Kylian Mbappe during a LaLiga match last year has been handed an 11-month suspended prison sentence after being convicted of a hate crime.

The suspension of the sentence is conditional on the unnamed fan not attending football stadiums for any official sports competitions for two years.

The individual has also been handed a fine along with “various disqualification penalties”, Real Madrid said in a statement.

“This ruling adds to the criminal convictions already issued for racist insults against Real Madrid players at the Mestalla, Son Moix, Vallecas, and José Zorrilla stadiums,” the club statement continued.

“Real Madrid, which has acted as a private prosecutor in this case and continues to do so in others involving similar incidents, reaffirms its commitment to combating racism and eradicating any racist behavior in football and sports.”

The incident occurred during Real Madrid’s 3-0 win over Real Oviedo at the Carlos Tartiere Stadium in August 2025, during which Mbappe bagged a brace.

Vinicius Jr, who has been persistently targeted with racist abuse at multiple stadiums in Spain as well as online, also scored in the match.

After the match, LaLiga reported alleged racist chanting towards Mbappe and Vinicius to Spain’s National Police, with the league alleging that chants imitating monkey sounds were heard on multiple occasions.

In March 2024, Vinicius broke down in tears during an emotional press conference as he bemoaned that racism was getting worse as perpetrators were going unpunished.

“I just want to play football but it’s hard to move forward… I feel less and less like playing (due to the racist abuse),” he said.

Gazza began a two-year spell at Middlesbrough in 1998

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

After six years in Italy and Scotland, Paul Gascoigne returned to English football in March 1998 when he signed for Middlesbrough.

At this stage of his career, Gazza was no longer the force of nature that lit up Italia 90 and Euro 96 as he body struggled to keep up the pace with his footballing brain.

However, his ability to be at the centre of attention and to entertain all around him, remained undiminished.

Former Boro goalkeeper Mark Schwarzer had a front row seat for all of Gazza’s pranks and hijinks - whether they lit up the dressing room, or left team-mates seeing red.

“Gazza has a heart of gold,” Schwarzer tells FourFourTwo. “All he wants to do is make people laugh, have fun and bring smiles to people’s faces.

“He’d do stuff that was outrageously funny and wrong, but there was never any malice.”

When Gascoigne arrived at the Riverside Stadium, he joined from Rangers at the tail end of a campaign which had seen him score just three goals in 28 games and while his impact had clearly diminished from his early ‘90s pomp, it was clear to Schwarzer that the ability was still there.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“On the pitch, he showed glimpses of the player he had been, but there was frustration because his mind wanted to do things his body couldn’t always keep up with,” he continues.

“What a player, though, and what a person to be around.”

As well as Gazza the player, the Boro squad also saw Gazza the character.

“Sometimes he’d come into training wearing the same clothes for days,” Schwarzer continues.

“One day, he took his socks off and went “Oh my God, these are horrendous”, then found Gianluca Festa’s Armani ones and swapped them for his own. Festa came back, realised what he’d done and started running around the building looking for him.

“When Festa exploded, he exploded, but he couldn’t find Gazza, thank goodness. Festa ended up going home with no socks, because there was no way he was wearing Gazza’s!”
